summary.text: Optical aberration is the way a lens or mirror fails to reproduce an object faithfully, leaving the image blurred, distorted or fringed with color.
It happens because light from one point of an object does not meet at a single point, since simple paraxial theory is only an approximation and not because of flaws in the lens.
Aberrations are either monochromatic, caused by geometry, or chromatic, caused by dispersion, and makers of optical instruments must correct for them.

facts.label: Chromatic cause
facts.value: Dispersion makes different wavelengths focus at different points

facts.label: Perfect lenses
facts.value: Even flawlessly made real lenses do not focus to a single point

facts.label: Defocus
facts.value: Usually not counted as an aberration, since moving the lens fixes it

facts.label: Piston and tilt
facts.value: Shift the focal point but still give a perfect image

items.prompt: A lens is ground and polished with perfect precision, yet its photos are not perfectly sharp at the edges. What is the likeliest explanation?

options.label: The simple ideal theory of lenses is only approximately true
The glass must have tiny cracks that cannot be seen
The lens needs a thicker coating of polish
The photographer's eyes add blur to the picture

items.explain: Real lenses, even perfectly made, do not focus light to a single point, because paraxial theory is not a completely accurate model.

items.prompt: A cheap magnifier shows a thin red and blue fringe around the edges of a black letter. What causes the fringe?

options.label: The ink reflects red light and blue light separately
Different wavelengths focus at different points because of dispersion
The magnifier is not curved enough at its centre
The glass is held too far from the page

items.explain: Chromatic aberration is caused by dispersion, the variation of refractive index with wavelength, so colors come to focus at different points.

items.prompt: A scientist lights a test target with a laser of one single color. Which aberration type disappears from her results?

options.label: The kind caused by the lens geometry
The kind seen in both lenses and mirrors
The kind that depends on wavelength
Neither type, since both come from the glass

items.explain: Chromatic aberration depends on dispersion and does not appear with monochromatic light, while monochromatic aberrations remain.

items.prompt: A photo is blurry only because the sensor sits slightly too far from where the lens focuses, and nudging the lens fixes it. How is this usually classed?

options.label: As a chromatic aberration from the glass's dispersion
As a monochromatic aberration from curved surfaces
As the worst of all the lens aberrations
Not as a lens aberration, since moving the lens corrects it

items.explain: Defocus is technically the lowest-order aberration but is usually not counted, because moving the lens or image plane brings the image to the focus.

items.prompt: An otherwise perfect wavefront is shifted by piston and tilt. What does the resulting image look like?

options.label: Perfect, but moved to a different position
Blurred in the same way as chromatic aberration
Split into several fringes of color
Distorted, as with every true aberration

items.explain: Piston and tilt only shift the focal point, so they are not true optical aberrations: the image stays aberration-free.

items.prompt: A lens designer opens the aperture wider to gather more light, and the image gets less sharp. What best explains this?

options.label: Wider openings always add extra color from the glass
The ideal theory only holds for rays at tiny angles to the axis
A bigger opening makes the lens thinner at its edges
Light cannot be focused once it exceeds a set brightness

items.explain: The ideal Gaussian theory holds only for rays close to the axis; when aperture or field of view grows past certain limits, uncorrected images become ill-defined and blurred.
